26565.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557) is a technique within the Credential Access and Collection tactics, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves positioning a system between networked devices by abusing protocols like ARP, DNS, or LLMNR to redirect traffic. This allows adversaries to intercept credentials such as passwords and session cookies, manipulate transmitted data, or conduct replay attacks. It is also used to establish positions for network sniffing or to perform downgrade attacks on communication protocols like SSL/TLS.

26568.name: AcidPour
26568.uncertain_mes: [AcidPour](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1167) is a variant of [AcidRain](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1125) designed to impact a wider range of x86 architecture Linux devices. [AcidPour](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1167) is an x86 ELF binary that expands on the targeted devices and locations in [AcidRain](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1125) by including items such as Unsorted Block Image (UBI), Deice Mapper (DM), and various flash memory references. Based on this expanded targeting, [AcidPour](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1167) can impact a variety of device types including IoT, networking, and ICS embedded device types.(Citation: SentinelOne AcidPour 2024) [AcidPour](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1167) is a wiping payload associated with the [Sandworm Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0034) threat actor, and potentially linked to attacks against Ukrainian internet service providers (ISPs) in 2023.(Citation: CERT-UA TelecomAttack 2023)
26568.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AcidPour is a wiper malware family, first observed in March 2024. It is related to AcidRain. Its key Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) include Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486), Service Stop (T1489), Account Access Removal (T1531), Indicator Removal (T1070), and Masquerading (T1036). It targets Ukraine and has been associated with infrastructure domains like solntsepek.ru, solntsepek.info, solntsepek.com, and solntsepek.org.[/profile]

26570.name: AcidRain
26570.uncertain_mes: [AcidRain](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1125) is an ELF binary targeting modems and routers using MIPS architecture.(Citation: AcidRain JAGS 2022) [AcidRain](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1125) is associated with the ViaSat KA-SAT communication outage that took place during the initial phases of the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Analysis indicates overlap with another network device-targeting malware, VPNFilter, associated with [Sandworm Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0034).(Citation: AcidRain JAGS 2022) US and European government sources linked [AcidRain](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1125) to Russian government entities, while Ukrainian government sources linked [AcidRain](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1125) specifically to [Sandworm Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0034).(Citation: AcidRain State Department 2022)(Citation: Vincens AcidPour 2024)
26570.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AcidRain is a data wiper malware family that targets routers, modems, and SATCOM equipment, notably used in a cyberattack against the KA-SAT satellite broadband service affecting Ukraine and Europe. Its technical behaviors align with the MITRE ATT&CK techniques for Account Access Removal (T1531), Service Stop (T1489), Indicator Removal (T1070), Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486), and Masquerading (T1036), indicating capabilities to disable accounts and services, delete forensic evidence, encrypt data, and disguise malicious files. Associated infrastructure includes domains like solntsepek.info and a SHA256 hash (6a8824048417abe156a16455b8e29170f8347312894fde2aabe644c4995d7728). It shares a SHA256 hash (13037b749aa4b1eda538fda26d6ac41c8f7b1d02d83f47b0d187dd645154e033) with entities like GraphSteel and HermeticWiper, suggesting potential code overlap or coordinated campaigns.[/profile]

26579.name: GreyEnergy - S0342
26579.uncertain_mes: [GreyEnergy](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0342) is a backdoor written in C and compiled in Visual Studio. [GreyEnergy](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0342) shares similarities with the [BlackEnergy](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0089) malware and is thought to be the successor of it.(Citation: ESET GreyEnergy Oct 2018)
26579.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GreyEnergy - S0342, also known as greyenergy, is a C-based backdoor compiled with Visual Studio and considered the successor to BlackEnergy. It is attributed to the Sandworm Team and Telebots group. Its key behaviors include modifying the Windows Registry for persistence and defense evasion, establishing command and control channels (TA0011), and using scheduled tasks for execution and persistence (TA0003). The malware primarily targets Windows platforms and has been used in attacks against entities in Estonia and Ukraine. Its infrastructure has included domains like nceess[.]com and IP addresses such as 79.141.168[.]137.[/profile]

26580.name: Kapeka
26580.uncertain_mes: Kapeka is a backdoor written in C++ used against victims in Eastern Europe since at least mid-2022. Kapeka has technical overlaps with [Exaramel for Windows](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0343) and [Prestige](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1058) malware variants, both of which are linked to [Sandworm Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0034). Kapeka may have been used in advance of [Prestige](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1058) deployment in late 2022.(Citation: WithSecure Kapeka 2024)(Citation: Microsoft KnuckleTouch 2024)
26580.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kapeka, also known as kapeka, is a backdoor attributed to the Sandworm Team. It is a C++ malware family active since at least mid-2022, used against targets in Eastern Europe, specifically Estonia and Ukraine. Its key behaviors include establishing command and control (TA0011) and achieving persistence via scheduled tasks (T1053, TA0003). It exhibits technical overlaps with Exaramel for Windows and Prestige malware and has reportedly been used as a precursor to destructive attacks.[/profile]

26583.name: TA0011
26583.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0011 is the Command and Control tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Adversaries establish communication channels with compromised systems to maintain control and relay instructions. This tactic is platform-agnostic and can leverage various infrastructures, including physical or cloud-based servers, to host command and control operations. Techniques under this tactic involve using custom communication protocols or abusing legitimate services like databases to facilitate covert data exchange and remote command execution.

26640.name: ShadowLink
26640.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ShadowLink is a malware attributed to the North Korean APT group Andariel. It is associated with exploiting vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-32315, CVE-2024-1709, CVE-2023-23397, CVE-2022-41352, and CVE-2021-34473. Its key TTPs involve Account Discovery, Account Manipulation, and Service Execution for persistence and privilege escalation, as well as using Remote Services for lateral movement and Data from Information Repositories for collection. It has targeted systems in Australia, Canada, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and the United States, using infrastructure such as the domains lt.tech-keys.com, hwupdates.com, cloud-sync.org, and support.csolve.net.[/profile]

26641.name: LocalOlive
26641.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LocalOlive is a malware with known aliases including Buterat, Cmoon, and LatentBot. It is attributed to unknown groups. Its key technical behaviors involve exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2024-1709, CVE-2023-32315, CVE-2023-23397, CVE-2022-41352, and CVE-2021-34473, and it uses TTPs like Data from Information Repositories, Account Manipulation, Account Discovery, Remote Services, and Service Execution. It targets platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, SaaS, and ESXi, and has been observed in locations such as Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, Ukraine, and the United States. Its associated infrastructure includes domains like lt.tech-keys.com, cloud-sync.org, hwupdates.com, and support.csolve.net.[/profile]

26670.name: OM.vbs
26670.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]OM.vbs is a Visual Basic Script (VBS) malware. It uses the Visual Basic programming language for execution and establishes command and control (C2) via encrypted channels and application layer protocols, specifically contacting the domain https://api.wordinfos.com. Its behaviors include credential theft from password stores and the use of remote access tools. It has been observed targeting systems in Iraq and potentially exploits vulnerabilities CVE-2025-27921 and CVE-2025-27920.[/profile]

26675.name: OMClientService.exe
26675.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]OMClientService.exe is a malware executable that exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-36884, CVE-2025-27921, and CVE-2025-27920. It uses techniques like Data from Information Repositories, Data Encoding, Data Staged, Exfiltration Over Web Service, and Encrypted Channel for its operations. Its command and control infrastructure involves the domain api.wordinfos.com. The malware has been associated with or shares infrastructure patterns with other malware families like Conti (linked to Wizard Spider) and IcedID (linked to Gold Cabin and Lunar Spider). It has targeted systems in Iraq.[/profile]

26676.name: OMServerService.exe
26676.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]OMServerService.exe is a malware executable. It is associated with the Conti ransomware (linked to Wizard Spider) and the IcedID malware (linked to Gold Cabin and Lunar Spider), as indicated by shared named pipes (e.g., \MSSE-3328-server). Its techniques include Data from Information Repositories, Data Staging, and Exfiltration Over Web Service for collection and theft, and it uses Data Encoding and Encrypted Channel for command-and-control obfuscation. It has targeted Iraq and uses infrastructure like api.wordinfos.com.[/profile]

26677.name: OMServerService.vbs
26677.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]OMServerService.vbs is a malware script that exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-36884, CVE-2025-27921, and CVE-2025-27920. Its key behaviors involve data collection from information repositories, staging collected data, and exfiltrating it over web services, while using data encoding and encrypted channels for command and control. It targets Windows systems and has been observed communicating with infrastructure such as api.wordinfos.com. The malware shares operational similarities with ransomware families like BlackCat, Babuk, and Diavol, particularly in its targeting of specific services and processes for disruption.[/profile]

26678.name: unkown_apt_group
26678.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely a subgroup or affiliate of the Doppel Spider/Indrik Spider ransomware operation (also known as Evil Corp or TA505), primarily uses the DoppelPaymer ransomware and a cluster of custom tools including OMClientService.exe, OMServerService.exe, OMServerService.vbs, and OM.vbs. Its key techniques involve Dynamic Resolution and Bidirectional Communication for resilient command and control, Data Staging for collection, and Data Encoding and Encrypted Channels for obfuscation, often leveraging infrastructure like api.wordinfos.com. The group exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-36884, CVE-2025-27921, and CVE-2025-27920. It has conducted attacks globally, with noted targeting in Kosovo, Moldova, Iraq, and the United States, and its primary motivation is financial gain through ransomware extortion.[/profile]

26684.name: DoppelPaymer
26684.uncertain_mes:
Taiwanese laptop maker Compal Electronics suffered a DoppelPaymer ransomware attack over the weekend, with the attackers demanding an almost $17 million ransom.
Compal is the second-largest original design manufacturer (ODM) of laptops globally, with well-known companies rebranding their devices or designs, including Apple, HP, Dell, Lenovo, and Acer.
$16.7 million ransom demanded
26684.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DoppelPaymer, also known as doppelpaymer and doppeldridex, is a ransomware attributed to groups like Doppel Spider, Indrik Spider, Evil Corp, and TA505. It employs techniques such as Dynamic Resolution (T1568) for C2 evasion, Bidirectional Communication (T1102.002) via web services, and Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068). It targets Windows platforms and uses JavaScript (T1059.007) for execution, maintaining blacklists of security software CRC32 hashes to avoid detection. Its infrastructure includes domains like api.wordinfos.com, and it has been used in attacks globally, including in Kosovo, Moldova, Iraq, and the United States.[/profile]

26689.name: Hide Artifacts
26689.description:
Adversaries may attempt to hide artifacts associated with their behaviors to evade detection. Operating systems may have features to hide various artifacts, such as important system files and administrative task execution, to avoid disrupting user work environments and prevent users from changing files or features on the system. Adversaries may abuse these features to hide artifacts such as files, directories, user accounts, or other system activity to evade detection.(Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan)(Citation: Cybereason OSX Pirrit)(Citation: MalwareBytes ADS July 2015)

Adversaries may also attempt to hide artifacts associated with malicious behavior by creating computing regions that are isolated from common security instrumentation, such as through the use of virtualization technology.(Citation: Sophos Ragnar May 2020)

Adversaries may abuse these features to hide artifacts such as files, directories, user accounts, or other system activity to evade detection.(Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan)(Citation: Cybereason OSX Pirrit)(Citation: MalwareBytes ADS July 2015)

Adversaries may also attempt to hide artifacts associated with malicious behavior by creating computing regions that are isolated from common security instrumentation, such as through the use of virtualization technology.(Citation: Sophos Ragnar May 2020)
26689.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Hide Artifacts is a Defense Evasion technique (ID: T1564) applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Office Suite platforms. It involves abusing built-in operating system features to conceal malicious files, directories, user accounts, or system activity from detection. This includes leveraging features designed to hide system files or administrative tasks, and can extend to using virtualization to isolate malicious behavior from security tools. The technique is distinct from network infrastructure hiding or simple indicator removal, focusing on the local concealment of digital artifacts.

26691.name: Apostle
26691.uncertain_mes: [Apostle](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1133) is malware that has functioned as both a wiper and, in more recent versions, as ransomware.  [Apostle](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1133) is written in .NET and shares various programming and functional overlaps with [IPsec Helper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1132).(Citation: SentinelOne Agrius 2021)
26691.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Apostle is a .NET malware family that functions as both a wiper and ransomware. It is also known as Apostle Loader or Jennlog Loader. It is attributed to threat groups Agrius and Pink Sandstorm. Its key behaviors include subverting trust controls, impairing defenses, inhibiting system recovery, and performing indicator removal (T1070) to delete forensic evidence. It establishes persistence via boot or logon autostart execution. Apostle shares significant programming and functional overlaps with related malware families IPsec Helper and ShellClient RAT.[/profile]

26692.name: Wiper
26692.uncertain_mes: [Wiper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0041) is a family of destructive malware used in March 2013 during breaches of South Korean banks and media companies. (Citation: Dell Wiper)
26692.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Wiper is a family of destructive malware, with aliases including MultiLayer Wiper and Bruh Wiper. It is associated with the Agrius group. Its key technical behaviors involve inhibiting system recovery (T1490) to prevent restoration after an attack, using boot or logon autostart execution (T1547) for persistence, and subverting trust controls (T1553) for defense evasion. It targets platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. The malware was notably used in breaches of South Korean banks and media companies in March 2013.[/profile]

26694.name: unkown_apt_group
26694.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the APT group Agrius, also known as the developer or user of the Wiper malware (aka MultiLayer Wiper, Bruh Wiper). Its key malware is the Wiper family, a destructive tool. Its key TTPs include Subvert Trust Controls (T1553), Inhibit System Recovery (T1490), Impair Defenses (T1562), and Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) for persistence and defense evasion. It is attributed to the Agrius group and has been used in attacks targeting South Korean banks and media. Its primary motivation appears to be destructive data attacks.[/profile]

26733.name: Disk Wipe
26733.description:
Adversaries may wipe or corrupt raw disk data on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. With direct write access to a disk, adversaries may attempt to overwrite portions of disk data. Adversaries may opt to wipe arbitrary portions of disk data and/or wipe disk structures like the master boot record (MBR). A complete wipe of all disk sectors may be attempted.

To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware used for wiping disks may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster Destructive Malware)

On network devices, adversaries may wipe configuration files and other data from the device using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `erase`.(Citation: erase_cmd_cisco)

26733.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Disk Wipe is a MITRE ATT&CK technique (ID: T1561) under the Impact tactic, targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries gaining direct write access to a storage device to overwrite arbitrary portions of disk data, including structures like the master boot record (MBR), to interrupt system availability. This can be performed via direct disk access, sometimes using third-party drivers like RawDisk, or on network devices using CLI commands such as `erase`. Malware implementing this may include worm-like features for propagation, leveraging techniques like Valid Accounts and OS Credential Dumping.[profile]

26738.name: AridSpy
26738.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AridSpy is a malware entity targeting users in Palestine and Egypt, with indicators including domains such as alwaysgoodidea.com, zezsoft.wuaze.com, pariberychat.com, almoshell.website, and renatchat.com. It is listed among other malware families like GhostRedirector, PlushDaemon, and AsyncRAT in threat intelligence contexts, and is associated with the group TA410. Key technical behaviors involve command and control via HTTPS and SMB beacons, with configurable parameters like sleeptime and jitter, and it uses specific infrastructure such as the server 91.215.85.143 on port 443.

26739.name: unkown_apt_group
26739.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the APT group known as Arid Viper, also commonly referred to as APT-C-23. Its key malware and tools include Arid Gopher (a Go-based variant of its core malware), Micropsia (a Delphi RAT), and AridSpy. Its key TTPs involve initial access via phishing (T1566), credential theft via input capture (T1056), lateral movement using remote services (T1021), and defense evasion through obfuscated files (T1027) and process injection (T1055). The group is attributed to and operates from the Middle East, with a primary targeting focus on Israel, and has also targeted entities in Palestine and Egypt. Its motivation is believed to be cyber espionage, with noted targeting of political entities such as Hamas opposition.[/profile]

26798.name: Uncommonly Used Port
26798.description: Adversaries may conduct C2 communications over a non-standard port to bypass proxies and firewalls that have been improperly configured.
26798.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may conduct C2 communications over a non-standard port to bypass proxies and firewalls that have been improperly configured.
26798.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Uncommonly Used Port is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1065 within the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries conducting command and control communications over a non-standard port to bypass improperly configured network proxies and firewalls. This technique is distinct from using commonly used ports for blending in, focusing instead on exploiting gaps in security configurations by selecting atypical port numbers for malicious traffic.

26801.name: Arid Gopher
26801.uncertain_mes: What is Arid Gopher? An Analysis of a New, Never-Before-Seen Malware Variant
26801.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Arid Gopher is a malware variant attributed to the Arid Viper group. It is functionally identical to the Arid Viper malware but is written in the Go programming language, with its V1 variant compiled using Go 1.16.5gs and incorporating code from public GitHub libraries. Its key behaviors include lateral movement via Remote Services (T1021), credential theft via Input Capture, initial access via Phishing (T1566), and defense evasion through Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027). It has been associated with infrastructure domains such as chloe-boreman.com, seomoi.net, and salimafia.net, and a C2 URL at http://5.182.39.44/esuzmwmrtajj/cmsnvbyawttf/mkxnhqwdywbu, with a primary targeting focus on Israel.[/profile]

26802.name: Micropsia
26802.uncertain_mes: [Micropsia](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0339) is a remote access tool written in Delphi.(Citation: Talos Micropsia June 2017)(Citation: Radware Micropsia July 2018)
26802.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Micropsia, also known as S0339, is a Delphi-written remote access tool (RAT) attributed to the APT-C-23 (also known as Arid Viper) threat group, which has targeted entities such as Hamas opposition. Its key technical behaviors include using Input Capture (T1056) for credential theft, employing Remote Services (T1021) for lateral movement, and utilizing Phishing (T1566) for initial access, while also employing Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) for defense evasion. It primarily targets Windows platforms and has been associated with infrastructure domains such as jumpstartmail.com, rnacgroup.com, paydayloansnew.com, seomoi.net, and chloe-boreman.com.[/profile]

26888.name: Salty2FA
26888.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Salty2FA is a malware with no known aliases and is not attributed to a specific group. Its key technical behaviors involve using Browser Session Hijacking (T1185) to potentially bypass 2-factor authentication, executing malicious payloads via System Binary Proxy Execution techniques like Msiexec (T1218.007), and employing Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557) tactics for credential interception. It targets Windows platforms and uses infrastructure including domains like marketplace24ei.ru and telephony.nexttradeitaly.com for command and control. It shares target keyword lists for credential theft (including terms for 2FA, crypto, and banking) with other stealers like Kematian Stealer, SilentPrism, and Rhadamanthys.[/profile]

26889.name: Tycoon2FA
26889.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Tycoon2FA is a malware that has been used in attacks targeting entities in the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States. Its technical behaviors include using the Adversary-in-the-Middle technique to intercept credentials, employing System Binary Proxy Execution via tools like Msiexec to evade defenses, performing System Checks to detect virtual environments, and utilizing Steganography to hide command and control traffic. Its infrastructure has been associated with domains such as telephony.nexttradeitaly.com, marketplace24ei.ru, and specific malicious URLs.[/profile]

26893.name: unkown_apt_group
26893.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the Rhadamanthys Stealer malware cluster, operates with aliases including Backdoordiplomacy, Backdip, Quarian, and Cloudcomputating. Its key malware includes Rhadamanthys Stealer, Salty2FA, and Tycoon2FA. Its technical profile is characterized by the use of Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks for credential theft, specifically to bypass two-factor authentication via Browser Session Hijacking, and employs Defense Evasion techniques such as System Binary Proxy Execution, notably abusing Msiexec. The group has staged infrastructure using domains like marketplace24ei.ru and telephony.nexttradeitaly.com. Its campaigns have primarily targeted entities in Western Europe, including the United Kingdom, France, Spain, Greece, and Switzerland, as well as North America (Canada and the United States), with a motivation focused on financial theft and credential harvesting.[profile]

26925.name: Browser Session Hijacking
26925.description:
Adversaries may take advantage of security vulnerabilities and inherent functionality in browser software to change content, modify user-behaviors, and intercept information as part of various browser session hijacking techniques.(Citation: Wikipedia Man in the Browser)

A specific example is when an adversary injects software into a browser that allows them to inherit cookies, HTTP sessions, and SSL client certificates of a user then use the browser as a way to pivot into an authenticated intranet.(Citation: Cobalt Strike Browser Pivot)(Citation: ICEBRG Chrome Extensions) Executing browser-based behaviors such as pivoting may require specific process permissions, such as `SeDebugPrivilege` and/or high-integrity/administrator rights.

Another example involves pivoting browser traffic from the adversary's browser through the user's browser by setting up a proxy which will redirect web traffic. This does not alter the user's traffic in any way, and the proxy connection can be severed as soon as the browser is closed. The adversary assumes the security context of whichever browser process the proxy is injected into. Browsers typically create a new process for each tab that is opened and permissions and certificates are separated accordingly. With these permissions, an adversary could potentially browse to any resource on an intranet, such as [Sharepoint](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/002) or webmail, that is accessible through the browser and which the browser has sufficient permissions. Browser pivoting may also bypass security provided by 2-factor authentication.(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)

26925.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Browser Session Hijacking is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1185 under the Collection tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. This method can also involve setting up a proxy to redirect the adversary's web traffic through the compromised browser process, potentially bypassing two-factor authentication and accessing internal resources like SharePoint or webmail.

26927.name: KTLVdoor
26927.uncertain_mes: - During our monitoring of the Chinese-speaking threat actor Earth Lusca, we discovered a new multiplatform backdoor written in Golang, named KTLVdoor, which has both Microsoft Windows and Linux versions.
26927.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]KTLVdoor, also known as ktlvdoor, is a multiplatform backdoor written in Golang with both Windows and Linux versions. It is attributed to the Chinese-speaking threat actor Earth Lusca. Its key behaviors include using web shells for persistence (T1505.003), performing timestomping (T1070.006) and system time discovery (T1124) for defense evasion and discovery, and potentially using SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) for lateral movement. It communicates with command-and-control servers via HTTP on IP addresses such as 182.92.155.149:81, 59.110.226.246:443, 121.40.70.23:443, 59.110.136.109:9999, and 106.14.175.235:443.[/profile]

26929.name: unkown_apt_group
26929.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the Chinese state-sponsored APT group known as menuPass (also known as APT10 and Stone Panda). Its key malware includes SodaMaster, a fileless downloader, and it has been observed using tools like Spyder and has infrastructure overlaps with ShadowPad. Its technical behaviors involve credential harvesting via Password Filter DLL and Security Account Manager (SAM) dumping, lateral movement via Software Deployment Tools, and defense evasion through timestomping (T1070.006) and system time discovery (T1124). The group is attributed to China and has targeted entities in multiple regions, including Thailand, Hungary, France, Taiwan, and the United States, with motivations consistent with cyber espionage.[/profile]

27145.name: RPipeCommander
27145.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RPipeCommander is a malware entity. It has been observed in locations including Thailand, Hungary, France, Taiwan, and the United States. Its technical behaviors involve using infrastructure such as the domain api.googleauthenticatoronline.com and the IP 45.76.165.227 to host payloads like wECqKe529r.png. Its associated attack patterns include the use of a Password Filter DLL (T1556.002) for credential access, acquiring server infrastructure (T1583.004), abusing Software Deployment Tools (T1072) for execution, performing System Service Discovery (T1007), and accessing the Security Account Manager (T1003.002) to extract credential hashes.[/profile]

27164.name: unkown_apt_group
27164.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the Chinese state-aligned group BackdoorDiplomacy (also known as BackDip, Quarian, or CloudComputating), has been observed using the ShadowPad modular backdoor and MASOL RAT. 27350.name: T1495
27350.description:
Adversaries may overwrite or corrupt the flash memory contents of system BIOS or other firmware in devices attached to a system in order to render them inoperable or unable to boot, thus denying the availability to use the devices and/or the system.(Citation: Symantec Chernobyl W95.CIH) Firmware is software that is loaded and executed from non-volatile memory on hardware devices in order to initialize and manage device functionality. These devices may include the motherboard, hard drive, or video cards.

In general, adversaries may manipulate, overwrite, or corrupt firmware in order to deny the use of the system or devices. For example, corruption of firmware responsible for loading the operating system for network devices may render the network devices inoperable.(Citation: dhs_threat_to_net_devices)(Citation: cisa_malware_orgs_ukraine) Depending on the device, this attack may also result in [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485).

27353.name: T1602
27353.description:
Adversaries may collect data related to managed devices from configuration repositories. Configuration repositories are used by management systems in order to configure, manage, and control data on remote systems. Configuration repositories may also facilitate remote access and administration of devices.

Adversaries may target these repositories in order to collect large quantities of sensitive system administration data. Data from configuration repositories may be exposed by various protocols and software and can store a wide variety of data, much of which may align with adversary Discovery objectives.(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: US-CERT TA17-156A SNMP Abuse 2017)

27355.name: T1599
27355.description:
Adversaries may bridge network boundaries by compromising perimeter network devices or internal devices responsible for network segmentation. Breaching these devices may enable an adversary to bypass restrictions on traffic routing that otherwise separate trusted and untrusted networks.

Devices such as routers and firewalls can be used to create boundaries between trusted and untrusted networks.  They achieve this by restricting traffic types to enforce organizational policy in an attempt to reduce the risk inherent in such connections.  Restriction of traffic can be achieved by prohibiting IP addresses, layer 4 protocol ports, or through deep packet inspection to identify applications.  To participate with the rest of the network, these devices can be directly addressable or transparent, but their mode of operation has no bearing on how the adversary can bypass them when compromised.

When an adversary takes control of such a boundary device, they can bypass its policy enforcement to pass normally prohibited traffic across the trust boundary between the two separated networks without hinderance.  By achieving sufficient rights on the device, an adversary can reconfigure the device to allow the traffic they want, allowing them to then further achieve goals such as command and control via [Multi-hop Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/003) or exfiltration of data via [Traffic Duplication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1020/001). Adversaries may also target internal devices responsible for network segmentation and abuse these in conjunction with [Internal Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/001) to achieve the same goals.(Citation: Kaspersky ThreatNeedle Feb 2021)  In the cases where a border device separates two separate organizations, the adversary can also facilitate lateral movement into new victim environments.

27359.uncertain_mes: This step is needed to overcome Android restrictions for third party applications to abuse Accessibility services.

It employs Defense Evasion techniques including Impair Defenses, Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, and Indicator Removal, and uses Data Encoding (T1132) and Asymmetric Cryptography for command and control. It has targeted systems in South Africa, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Eswatini, and has been observed exploiting vulnerabilities including CVE-2021-26855, CVE-2021-26857, CVE-2021-26858, and CVE-2021-27065. 27361.name: unkown_apt_group
27361.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with or overlapping the group known as BackdoorDiplomacy (also aliased as BackDip, Quarian, and CloudComputating), operates with a focus on resource development and stealthy command and control. 27364.name: HUI Loader
27364.uncertain_mes: [HUI Loader](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1097) is a custom DLL loader that has been used since at least 2015 by China-based threat groups including [Cinnamon Tempest](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1021) and [menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045) to deploy malware on compromised hosts. [HUI Loader](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1097) has been observed in campaigns loading [SodaMaster](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0627), [PlugX](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0013), [Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154), [Komplex](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0162), and several strains of ransomware.(Citation: SecureWorks BRONZE STARLIGHT Ransomware Operations June 2022)
27364.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]HUI Loader, also known as hui loader, is a custom DLL loader malware family attributed to China-based threat groups including Cinnamon Tempest, menuPass, APT10, Blue Termite, A41APT, and DEV-0401. It employs Defense Evasion techniques like Masquerading (T1036) and Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) to load secondary payloads such as SodaMaster, PlugX, Cobalt Strike, Komplex, PoisonIvy, Quasar, and ransomware. Its infrastructure includes domains like miscrosofts.com and www.100helpchat.com, and it distributes payloads via aliased URLs like those on aliyuncs.com.[/profile]

27365.name: unkown_apt_group
27365.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the Cinnamon Tempest group (also known as backdoordiplomacy, backdip, quarian, and cloudcomputating), employs key malware including the custom Cheerscrypt ransomware—derived from leaked Babuk source code for ESXi and Windows—and leverages common tools like Cobalt Strike and Impacket. Its technical behaviors involve data exfiltration over alternative protocols (T1048) and web services (T1567), data encoding (T1132), and account discovery (T1087) for lateral movement and collection from network shares. The group's infrastructure overlaps with Night Sky ransomware deployments and uses domains such as duckducklive.top, kaspresksy.com, and microsofts.net. It is believed to be of likely Chinese origin, targeting ESXi and Windows environments, with motivations centered on data theft and ransomware deployment.[/profile]

27404.name: Cheerscrypt ransomware
27404.uncertain_mes: [Cheerscrypt](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1096) is a ransomware that was developed by [Cinnamon Tempest](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1021) and has been used in attacks against ESXi and Windows environments since at least 2022. [Cheerscrypt](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1096) was derived from the leaked [Babuk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0638) source code and has infrastructure overlaps with deployments of Night Sky ransomware, which was also derived from [Babuk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0638).(Citation: Sygnia Emperor Dragonfly October 2022)(Citation: Trend Micro Cheerscrypt May 2022)
27404.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cheerscrypt ransomware, also known as Cheerscrypt, is attributed to the Cinnamon Tempest group and is derived from the leaked Babuk source code, specifically its ESXi encryptor. It employs techniques including Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048), Data Encoding (T1132), Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570), Account Discovery (T1087), and Non-Application Layer Protocol (T1095) for command and control. The ransomware primarily targets ESXi and Windows environments and has infrastructure overlaps with deployments of the Night Sky ransomware.[/profile]

27405.name: Impacket
27405.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Impacket is a collection of Python classes for working with network protocols, not a malware family but a legitimate toolkit often weaponized. Its tools, such as WmiExec and secretsdump, are used by threat actors for lateral movement (T1021), account discovery (T1087), and data collection from network shares (T1039). Associated groups include APT10, APT32, Anunak, and Gallium. It facilitates activities like dumping Active Directory databases and can support data exfiltration over web services (T1567) and command-and-control traffic obfuscation via data encoding.[/profile]

27463.name: WezRat
27463.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]WezRat is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) malware. Its key technical behaviors include using the Compile After Delivery (T1027.004) technique for defense evasion, collecting Clipboard Data (T1115), and employing Data Encoding (T1132) for command-and-control obfuscation. It establishes persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) and performs credential access by searching for Credentials In Files (T1552.001). Its known infrastructure includes domains like onlinelive.info, connect.il-cert.net, il-cert.net, and il-cert.org.il, and it has been observed targeting entities in Sweden, France, Israel, and the United States.[/profile]

27465.name: unkown_apt_group
27465.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the MuddyWater APT group (also known as Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros, or Cobalt Ulster), primarily uses the WezRat Remote Access Trojan (RAT) as its key malware. Its infrastructure includes domains like onlinelive.info, connect.il-cert.net, il-cert.net, and il-cert.org.il. The group has targeted entities in Sweden, France, Israel, and the United States and shows overlaps with other clusters like BackdoorDiplomacy. It is widely attributed to Iran, with motivations typically aligned with espionage and data theft.

27488.name: CacheHttp

The malware has been observed using infrastructure with domains such as iqwebservice.com, asiacall.net, mail.miicrosoft.com, mofaiq.com, and spacenet.fun, which have been associated with targeting Iraq.[/profile]

27489.name: Veaty

27490.name: Spearal

27492.name: unkown_apt_group
27492.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is attributed to the Iranian state-sponsored APT group OilRig (also known as APT34 and Earth Simnavaz). It employs custom malware including STEALHOOK, QUADAGENT, and Helminth for data exfiltration, credential theft, and backdoor access, and has exploited vulnerability CVE-2024-30088. 27511.name: T1090.004
27511.description:
Adversaries may take advantage of routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) and other services which host multiple domains to obfuscate the intended destination of HTTPS traffic or traffic tunneled through HTTPS. (Citation: Fifield Blocking Resistent Communication through domain fronting 2015) Domain fronting involves using different domain names in the SNI field of the TLS header and the Host field of the HTTP header. If both domains are served from the same CDN, then the CDN may route to the address specified in the HTTP header after unwrapping the TLS header. A variation of the the technique, "domainless" fronting, utilizes a SNI field that is left blank; this may allow the fronting to work even when the CDN attempts to validate that the SNI and HTTP Host fields match (if the blank SNI fields are ignored).

For example, if domain-x and domain-y are customers of the same CDN, it is possible to place domain-x in the TLS header and domain-y in the HTTP header. Traffic will appear to be going to domain-x, however the CDN may route it to domain-y.

It works by abusing Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) that host multiple domains, using different domain names in the TLS SNI field and the HTTP Host header to route traffic to a hidden, adversary-controlled domain while appearing to connect to a benign front domain. A variation called "domainless" fronting uses a blank SNI field to bypass CDN validation checks. This technique is a sub-technique of Proxy (T1090) and has been associated with groups like APT29.[/profile]

27514.uncertain_mes: [Helminth](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0170) is a backdoor that has at least two variants - one written in VBScript and PowerShell that is delivered via a macros in Excel spreadsheets, and one that is a standalone Windows executable. (Citation: Palo Alto OilRig May 2016)

27594.name: T1127
27594.description:
Adversaries may take advantage of trusted developer utilities to proxy execution of malicious payloads. There are many utilities used for software development related tasks that can be used to execute code in various forms to assist in development, debugging, and reverse engineering.(Citation: engima0x3 DNX Bypass)(Citation: engima0x3 RCSI Bypass)(Citation: Exploit Monday WinDbg)(Citation: LOLBAS Tracker) These utilities may often be signed with legitimate certificates that allow them to execute on a system and proxy execution of malicious code through a trusted process that effectively bypasses application control solutions.

Smart App Control is a feature of Windows that blocks applications it considers potentially malicious from running by verifying unsigned applications against a known safe list from a Microsoft cloud service before executing them.(Citation: Microsoft Smart App Control) However, adversaries may leverage "reputation hijacking" to abuse an operating system’s trust of safe, signed applications that support the execution of arbitrary code. By leveraging [Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1127) to run their malicious code, adversaries may bypass Smart App Control protections.(Citation: Elastic Security Labs)

27594.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution, identified as T1127, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves adversaries abusing trusted, signed developer utilities (like MSBuild) to proxy the execution of malicious payloads. This method allows arbitrary code to run through a legitimate, trusted process, effectively bypassing application control and security solutions such as Windows Smart App Control by hijacking the system's trust in these signed binaries.[/profile]

27628.name: T1547.008
27628.description:
Adversaries may modify or add LSASS drivers to obtain persistence on compromised systems. The Windows security subsystem is a set of components that manage and enforce the security policy for a computer or domain. The Local Security Authority (LSA) is the main component responsible for local security policy and user authentication. The LSA includes multiple dynamic link libraries (DLLs) associated with various other security functions, all of which run in the context of the LSA Subsystem Service (LSASS) lsass.exe process.(Citation: Microsoft Security Subsystem)

Adversaries may target LSASS drivers to obtain persistence. By either replacing or adding illegitimate drivers (e.g., [Hijack Execution Flow](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574)), an adversary can use LSA operations to continuously execute malicious payloads.

This provides a stealthy mechanism for maintaining access on a compromised host.[/profile]

27641.name: Data from Cloud Storage
27641.description:
Adversaries may access data from cloud storage.

Many IaaS providers offer solutions for online data object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Storage, and Google Cloud Storage. Similarly, SaaS enterprise platforms such as Office 365 and Google Workspace provide cloud-based document storage to users through services such as OneDrive and Google Drive, while SaaS application providers such as Slack, Confluence, Salesforce, and Dropbox may provide cloud storage solutions as a peripheral or primary use case of their platform. 

In some cases, as with IaaS-based cloud storage, there exists no overarching application (such as SQL or Elasticsearch) with which to interact with the stored objects: instead, data from these solutions is retrieved directly though the [Cloud API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/009). In SaaS applications, adversaries may be able to collect this data directly from APIs or backend cloud storage objects, rather than through their front-end application or interface (i.e., [Data from Information Repositories](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213)). 

Adversaries may collect sensitive data from these cloud storage solutions. Providers typically offer security guides to help end users configure systems, though misconfigurations are a common problem.(Citation: Amazon S3 Security, 2019)(Citation: Microsoft Azure Storage Security, 2019)(Citation: Google Cloud Storage Best Practices, 2019) There have been numerous incidents where cloud storage has been improperly secured, typically by unintentionally allowing public access to unauthenticated users, overly-broad access by all users, or even access for any anonymous person outside the control of the Identity Access Management system without even needing basic user permissions.

This open access may expose various types of sensitive data, such as credit cards, personally identifiable information, or medical records.(Citation: Trend Micro S3 Exposed PII, 2017)(Citation: Wired Magecart S3 Buckets, 2019)(Citation: HIPAA Journal S3 Breach, 2017)(Citation: Rclone-mega-extortion_05_2021)

Adversaries may also obtain then abuse leaked credentials from source repositories, logs, or other means as a way to gain access to cloud storage objects.

27642.name: Establish Accounts
27642.description:
Adversaries may create and cultivate accounts with services that can be used during targeting. Adversaries can create accounts that can be used to build a persona to further operations. Persona development consists of the development of public information, presence, history and appropriate affiliations. This development could be applied to social media, website, or other publicly available information that could be referenced and scrutinized for legitimacy over the course of an operation using that persona or identity.(Citation: NEWSCASTER2014)(Citation: BlackHatRobinSage)

For operations incorporating social engineering, the utilization of an online persona may be important. These personas may be fictitious or impersonate real people. The persona may exist on a single site or across multiple sites (ex: Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter, Google, GitHub, Docker Hub, etc.). Establishing a persona may require development of additional documentation to make them seem real. This could include filling out profile information, developing social networks, or incorporating photos.(Citation: NEWSCASTER2014)(Citation: BlackHatRobinSage)

Establishing accounts can also include the creation of accounts with email providers, which may be directly leveraged for [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566).(Citation: Mandiant APT1) In addition, establishing accounts may allow adversaries to abuse free services, such as registering for trial periods to [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) for malicious purposes.(Citation: Free Trial PurpleUrchin)

27643.name: Fallback Channels
27643.description: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.
27643.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

It involves adversaries establishing backup or alternate communication channels to maintain C2 reliability if the primary channel is compromised or blocked, and to avoid data transfer thresholds. This technique is often used in conjunction with multi-stage channels (T1104) where a loader may have backup callbacks, and it has been employed by groups like FIN7, APT41, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

27684.name: Office Template Macros
27684.description:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office templates to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Microsoft Office contains templates that are part of common Office applications and are used to customize styles. The base templates within the application are used each time an application starts. (Citation: Microsoft Change Normal Template) Office Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros (Citation: MSDN VBA in Office) can be inserted into the base template and used to execute code when the respective Office application starts in order to obtain persistence. Examples for both Word and Excel have been discovered and published. By default, Word has a Normal.dotm template created that can be modified to include a malicious macro. Excel does not have a template file created by default, but one can be added that will automatically be loaded.(Citation: enigma0x3 normal.dotm)(Citation: Hexacorn Office Template Macros) Shared templates may also be stored and pulled from remote locations.(Citation: GlobalDotName Jun 2019) Word Normal.dotm location:
`C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm` Excel Personal.xlsb location:
`C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Excel\XLSTART\PERSONAL.XLSB` Adversaries may also change the location of the base template to point to their own by hijacking the application's search order, e.g. Word 2016 will first look for Normal.dotm under `C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\`, or by modifying the GlobalDotName registry key. By modifying the GlobalDotName registry key an adversary can specify an arbitrary location, file name, and file extension to use for the template that will be loaded on application startup. To abuse GlobalDotName, adversaries may first need to register the template as a trusted document or place it in a trusted location.(Citation: GlobalDotName Jun 2019) An adversary may need to enable macros to execute unrestricted depending on the system or enterprise security policy on use of macros.

27717.name: Credentials in Registry
27717.description:
Adversaries may search the Registry on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials. The Windows Registry stores configuration information that can be used by the system or other programs. Adversaries may query the Registry looking for credentials and passwords that have been stored for use by other programs or services. Sometimes these credentials are used for automatic logons.

Example commands to find Registry keys related to password information: (Citation: Pentestlab Stored Credentials)

* Local Machine Hive: `reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s`
* Current User Hive: `reg query HKCU /f password /t REG_SZ /s`

27719.name: System Location Discovery
27719.description:
Adversaries may gather information in an attempt to calculate the geographical location of a victim host. Adversaries may use the information from [System Location Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1614) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions.

Adversaries may attempt to infer the location of a system using various system checks, such as time zone, keyboard layout, and/or language settings.(Citation: FBI Ragnar Locker 2020)(Citation: Sophos Geolocation 2016)(Citation: Bleepingcomputer RAT malware 2020) Windows API functions such as `GetLocaleInfoW` can also be used to determine the locale of the host.(Citation: FBI Ragnar Locker 2020) In cloud environments, an instance's availability zone may also be discovered by accessing the instance metadata service from the instance.(Citation: AWS Instance Identity Documents)(Citation: Microsoft Azure Instance Metadata 2021)

Adversaries may also attempt to infer the location of a victim host using IP addressing, such as via online geolocation IP-lookup services.(Citation: Securelist Trasparent Tribe 2020)(Citation: Sophos Geolocation 2016)

It involves adversaries attempting to calculate a victim host's geographical location to inform follow-on actions. Technical mechanics include checking system settings like time zone, keyboard layout, and language, using Windows API functions such as GetLocaleInfoW, querying cloud instance metadata services for availability zones, and performing IP geolocation lookups via online services.

27723.name: Charon

28042.name: T1208
28042.uncertain_mes:
Service principal names (SPNs) are used to uniquely identify each instance of a Windows service. To enable authentication, Kerberos requires that SPNs be associated with at least one service logon account (an account specifically tasked with running a service (Citation: Microsoft Detecting Kerberoasting Feb 2018)). (Citation: Microsoft SPN) (Citation: Microsoft SetSPN) (Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014) (Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

Adversaries possessing a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) may request one or more Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) service tickets for any SPN from a domain controller (DC). (Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016) (Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015) Portions of these tickets may be encrypted with the RC4 algorithm, meaning the Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash of the service account associated with the SPN is used as the private key and is thus vulnerable to offline [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) attacks that may expose plaintext credentials. (Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015) (Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016) (Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

This same attack could be executed using service tickets captured from network traffic. (Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)

Cracked hashes may enable Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and  Lateral Movement via access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078). (Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)
28042.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1208, also known as Kerberoasting, is a Credential Access technique targeting Windows platforms. It involves an adversary with a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) requesting Kerberos service tickets (TGS) for Service Principal Names (SPNs) from a domain controller. Portions of these tickets, often encrypted with the vulnerable RC4 algorithm, contain the service account's Kerberos hash, which can be extracted and subjected to offline brute-force attacks to recover plaintext credentials. Cracked credentials facilitate persistence, privilege escalation, and lateral movement via valid accounts.

It primarily targets email clients such as Outlook and The Bat! to steal credentials and related account information, and its associated tool PteroCookie steals cookies from browsers including Opera, Firefox, Chrome, and Edge. Its key TTPs involve data collection from removable media (T1025), data staging (T1074), and stealing web session cookies (T1539), with command-and-control traffic using standard encoding schemes (T1132.001) like Base64. It targets Windows systems and has been associated with infrastructure domains such as lokalut.ru and rieturc.ru, with victim locations including Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Poland, and Ukraine.[/profile]

28710.name: PteroScreen
28710.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PteroScreen is a malware that uses the C2 domain youdad.ru and has been observed targeting Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Poland, and Ukraine. Its technical behaviors include data collection from removable media (T1025), staging collected data (T1074), and stealing web session cookies (T1539). For command and control, it employs data encoding techniques, specifically standard encoding (T1132.001), to obfuscate its traffic.[/profile]

28711.name: PteroRisk
28711.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PteroRisk is a malware targeting Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Poland, and Ukraine, with indicators of compromise including domains like amasiyagi.ru, dfgqdsd.ru, marginisbi.ru, rieturc.ru, and statuesque.ru. Its key tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) involve Data from Removable Media (T1025) for collection, Data Staged (T1074) to consolidate stolen files, Steal Web Session Cookie (T1539) for credential access, and command-and-control obfuscation via Standard Encoding (T1132.001) such as Base64 or ASCII.[/profile]

28712.name: PteroTemplate
28712.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PteroTemplate is a malware that uses remote template documents for payload delivery, as seen in related samples like PowerShower. Its technical behaviors include data staging (T1074), stealing web session cookies (T1539), and data collection from removable media (T1025). It targets systems in Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Poland, and Ukraine, and uses domains like rieturc.ru, statuesque.ru, and amasiyagi.ru for its infrastructure.[/profile]

28713.name: PteroDoc
28713.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PteroDoc is a malware entity. It is associated with the TWISTED SPIDER threat group. Its known infrastructure includes domains such as marginisbi.ru, www.toorisugita.ru, nododru.ru, havxcq.ru, and amasiyagi.ru, and it has been observed targeting systems in Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Poland, and Ukraine.[/profile]

28714.name: PteroX

28754.name: T1074.001
28754.description:
Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location or directory on the local system prior to Exfiltration. Data may be kept in separate files or combined into one file through techniques such as [Archive Collected Data](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1560). Interactive command shells may be used, and common functionality within [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) and bash may be used to copy data into a staging location.

Adversaries may also stage collected data in various available formats/locations of a system, including local storage databases/repositories or the Windows Registry.(Citation: Prevailion DarkWatchman 2021)

28765.name: GammaLoad

28782.name: GammaSteel
28782.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GammaSteel is a malware variant attributed to the Gamaredon APT group (also associated with Operation Armageddon). Its technical behaviors include establishing persistence via Windows Registry autostart execution (T1547) and employing defense evasion techniques like Indicator Blocking (T1562.006). It communicates with command-and-control infrastructure, including domains like position.crudoes.ru and various trycloudflare.com subdomains.[/profile]

28876.name: Indicator Blocking
28876.description:
An adversary may attempt to block indicators or events typically captured by sensors from being gathered and analyzed. This could include maliciously redirecting(Citation: Microsoft Lamin Sept 2017) or even disabling host-based sensors, such as Event Tracing for Windows (ETW)(Citation: Microsoft About Event Tracing 2018), by tampering settings that control the collection and flow of event telemetry.(Citation: Medium Event Tracing Tampering 2018) These settings may be stored on the system in configuration files and/or in the Registry as well as being accessible via administrative utilities such as [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) or [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047).

For example, adversaries may modify the `File` value in `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\Security` to hide their malicious actions in a new or different .evtx log file. This action does not require a system reboot and takes effect immediately.(Citation: disable_win_evt_logging) 

ETW interruption can be achieved multiple ways, however most directly by defining conditions using the [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) `Set-EtwTraceProvider` cmdlet or by interfacing directly with the Registry to make alterations.

In the case of network-based reporting of indicators, an adversary may block traffic associated with reporting to prevent central analysis. This may be accomplished by many means, such as stopping a local process responsible for forwarding telemetry and/or creating a host-based firewall rule to block traffic to specific hosts responsible for aggregating events, such as security information and event management (SIEM) products.

In Linux environments, adversaries may disable or reconfigure log processing tools such as syslog or nxlog to inhibit detection and monitoring capabilities to facilitate follow on behaviors. (Citation: LemonDuck) ESXi also leverages syslog, which can be reconfigured via commands such as `esxcli system syslog config set` and `esxcli system syslog config reload`.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022)(Citation: Broadcom Configuring syslog on ESXi)

28880.name: unkown_apt_group
28880.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the financially motivated threat group FIN6 or the broader Cobalt Group, is also known to operate under the aliases backdoordiplomacy, backdip, quarian, and cloudcomputating. 28920.name: T1016.001
28920.description:
Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems. This may be performed during automated discovery and can be accomplished in numerous ways such as using [Ping](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0097), `tracert`, and GET requests to websites, or performing initial speed testing to confirm bandwidth.

Adversaries may use the results and responses from these requests to determine if the system is capable of communicating with their C2 servers before attempting to connect to them. The results may also be used to identify routes, redirectors, and proxy servers.

28923.name: unkown_apt_group
28923.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This unknown APT group, suspected to be linked to or overlapping with the group known as BackdoorDiplomacy (also aliased Backdip, Quarian, and CloudComputating), operates across Southeast Asia and the Pacific, targeting entities in Fiji, Thailand, the Philippines, and Taiwan. Its technical profile includes the use of common post-exploitation techniques such as dumping credentials from LSASS memory (T1003.001), bypassing User Account Control (T1548.002), and executing commands via Windows services (T1569.002). The group has also been observed using exploitation for privilege escalation (T1068) and masquerading files to match legitimate names or locations (T1036.005). Its infrastructure has involved domains like dns.eudnslog.com, www.updateforhours.com, evnpowerspeedtest.com, and asis.downloadwindowsupdate.co. The group's motivation appears to be espionage, focusing on governmental and diplomatic entities within its target regions.[/profile]

28965.name: K4Spreader
28965.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]K4Spreader is a malware known to create hidden files in the /dev/ and /dev/shm/ directories, a behavior shared with malware families like KAIJI and GSOCKET. It exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2020-14883, CVE-2017-10271, and CVE-2023-46604. Its TTPs involve Remote Services, Brute Force, SSH, Remote System Discovery, and External Remote Services for initial access, credential access, and lateral movement. Associated infrastructure includes domains like c4k-ircd.pwndns.pw and IPs such as 154.213.192.44, and it has been observed targeting systems in Brazil and China.[/profile]

28966.name: PwnRig
28966.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PwnRig is a cryptocurrency miner malware targeting Brazil and China. It is associated with the 8220 Gang and uses the pwn.givemexyz[.]in domain as a failover IRC server for the Tsunami botnet. Its key behaviors include brute forcing credentials (T1110) and leveraging remote services like SSH (T1021.004) for initial access and lateral movement. It exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2020-14883, and CVE-2023-46604. Its infrastructure includes the indicator play.sck-dns.cc.[/profile]

28967.name: Hadooken
28967.uncertain_mes:
Hackers are targeting Oracle WebLogic servers to infect them with a new Linux malware named "Hadooken," which launches a cryptominer and a tool for distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks.

28969.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely the 8220 Gang, also known as Backdoordiplomacy, Backdip, Quarian, and Cloudcomputating, primarily uses malware such as Hadooken, Tsunami, PwnRig, and XMRig, often exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2020-14883, and CVE-2023-46604 in Oracle WebLogic servers. Its key TTPs include Process Hollowing and Portable Executable Injection for defense evasion, and Data Obfuscation for command and control. The group is attributed to actors in China and Brazil, targeting cloud and container environments globally for cryptojacking and DDoS attacks, with a primary motivation of financial gain through resource hijacking.[/profile]

29098.name: Hidden Window
29098.description:
Adversaries may use hidden windows to conceal malicious activity from the plain sight of users. In some cases, windows that would typically be displayed when an application carries out an operation can be hidden. This may be utilized by system administrators to avoid disrupting user work environments when carrying out administrative tasks. 

Adversaries may abuse these functionalities to hide otherwise visible windows from users so as not to alert the user to adversary activity on the system.(Citation: Antiquated Mac Malware)

On macOS, the configurations for how applications run are listed in property list (plist) files. One of the tags in these files can be `apple.awt.UIElement`, which allows for Java applications to prevent the application's icon from appearing in the Dock. A common use for this is when applications run in the system tray, but don't also want to show up in the Dock.

Similarly, on Windows there are a variety of features in scripting languages, such as [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001), Jscript, and [Visual Basic](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/005) to make windows hidden. One example of this is `powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden`.(Citation: PowerShell About 2019)

The Windows Registry can also be edited to hide application windows from the current user. For example, by setting the `WindowPosition` subkey in the `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Console\%SystemRoot%_System32_WindowsPowerShell_v1.0_PowerShell.exe` Registry key to a maximum value, PowerShell windows will open off screen and be hidden.(Citation: Cantoris Computing)

In addition, Windows supports the `CreateDesktop()` API that can create a hidden desktop window with its own corresponding `explorer.exe` process.(Citation: Hidden VNC)(Citation: Anatomy of an hVNC Attack)  All applications running on the hidden desktop window, such as a hidden VNC (hVNC) session,(Citation: Hidden VNC) will be invisible to other desktops windows.

Adversaries may also leverage cmd.exe(Citation: Cybereason - Hidden Malicious Remote Access) as a parent process, and then utilize a LOLBin, such as DeviceCredentialDeployment.exe,(Citation: LOLBAS Project GitHub Device Cred Dep)(Citation: SecureList BlueNoroff Device Cred Dev) to hide windows.

29154.name: T1598.003
29154.description:
Adversaries may send spearphishing messages with a malicious link to elicit sensitive information that can be used during targeting. Spearphishing for information is an attempt to trick targets into divulging information, frequently credentials or other actionable information. Spearphishing for information frequently involves social engineering techniques, such as posing as a source with a reason to collect information (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)) and/or sending multiple, seemingly urgent messages.

All forms of spearphishing are electronically delivered social engineering targeted at a specific individual, company, or industry. In this scenario, the malicious emails contain links generally accompanied by social engineering text to coax the user to actively click or copy and paste a URL into a browser.(Citation: TrendMictro Phishing)(Citation: PCMag FakeLogin) The given website may be a clone of a legitimate site (such as an online or corporate login portal) or may closely resemble a legitimate site in appearance and have a URL containing elements from the real site. URLs may also be obfuscated by taking advantage of quirks in the URL schema, such as the acceptance of integer- or hexadecimal-based hostname formats and the automatic discarding of text before an “@” symbol: for example, `hxxp://google.com@1157586937`.(Citation: Mandiant URL Obfuscation 2023)

Adversaries may also embed “tracking pixels,” "web bugs," or "web beacons" within phishing messages to verify the receipt of an email, while also potentially profiling and tracking victim information such as IP address.(Citation: NIST Web Bug)(Citation: Ryte Wiki) These mechanisms often appear as small images (typically one pixel in size) or otherwise obfuscated objects and are typically delivered as HTML code containing a link to a remote server.(Citation: Ryte Wiki)(Citation: IAPP)

Adversaries may also be able to spoof a complete website using what is known as a "browser-in-the-browser" (BitB) attack. By generating a fake browser popup window with an HTML-based address bar that appears to contain a legitimate URL (such as an authentication portal), they may be able to prompt users to enter their credentials while bypassing typical URL verification methods.(Citation: ZScaler BitB 2020)(Citation: Mr. D0x BitB 2022)

Adversaries can use phishing kits such as `EvilProxy` and `Evilginx2` to perform adversary-in-the-middle phishing by proxying the connection between the victim and the legitimate website. On a successful login, the victim is redirected to the legitimate website, while the adversary captures their session cookie (i.e., [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)) in addition to their username and password. This may enable the adversary to then bypass MFA via [Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/004).(Citation: Proofpoint Human Factor)

Adversaries may also send a malicious link in the form of Quick Response (QR) Codes (also known as “quishing”). These links may direct a victim to a credential phishing page.(Citation: QR-campaign-energy-firm) By using a QR code, the URL may not be exposed in the email and may thus go undetected by most automated email security scans.(Citation: qr-phish-agriculture) These QR codes may be scanned by or delivered directly  to a user’s mobile device (i.e., [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1660)), which may be less secure in several relevant ways.(Citation: qr-phish-agriculture) For example, mobile users may not be able to notice minor differences between genuine and credential harvesting websites due to mobile’s smaller form factor.

From the fake website, information is gathered in web forms and sent to the adversary. Adversaries may also use information from previous reconnaissance efforts (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)) to craft persuasive and believable lures.

29154.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Spearphishing Link, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1598.003, is a Reconnaissance technique on the PRE platform. It involves sending targeted emails with malicious links to elicit sensitive information, often using social engineering to pose as a trusted source. 29184.name: Pikabot
29184.uncertain_mes: [Pikabot](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1145) is a backdoor used for initial access and follow-on tool deployment active since early 2023. [Pikabot](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1145) is notable for extensive use of multiple encoding, encryption, and defense evasion mechanisms to evade defenses and avoid analysis. [Pikabot](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1145) has some overlaps with [QakBot](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0650), but insufficient evidence exists to definitively link these two malware families. [Pikabot](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1145) is frequently used to deploy follow on tools such as [Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) or ransomware variants.(Citation: Zscaler Pikabot 2023)(Citation: Elastic Pikabot 2024)(Citation: Logpoint Pikabot 2024)
29184.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Pikabot (also known as pikabot) is a backdoor malware family active since early 2023, attributed to the threat actor TA577. It is used for initial access and follow-on tool deployment, frequently delivering payloads like Cobalt Strike or ransomware. Its key technical behaviors include extensive use of multiple encoding, encryption, and defense evasion mechanisms to avoid analysis and detection. It overlaps with QakBot but is considered distinct. It primarily targets Windows platforms and operates via command-and-control infrastructure, as indicated by associated network indicators.[/profile]

29186.name: unkown_apt_group
29186.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, whose standardized APT group name is unknown but shows overlaps with the group known as BackdoorDiplomacy (also known as BackDip, Quarian, and CloudComputating), employs key techniques including Brute Force (T1110), Phishing (T1566), OS Credential Dumping (T1003), and the abuse of Valid Accounts (T1078) for initial access, credential theft, and lateral movement. Its operational infrastructure has been linked to indicators such as HTTP servers at IPs including 176.123.2.146, 89.117.2.34, and 155.94.208.137. The group's TTPs suggest a focus on credential access and persistence, utilizing publicly available tools for network propagation. While specific origin, target sectors, and primary motivation are not detailed in the provided data, its association with BackdoorDiplomacy implies potential state-aligned espionage objectives.[/profile]

29228.name: unkown_apt_group
29228.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the Chinese state-sponsored group known as Volt Typhoon, also known as Bronze Silhouette, Vanguard Panda, and Insidious Taurus. Its key malware is the KV Botnet, which targets end-of-life network appliances like Cisco RV320/325 routers for initial access and persistence. Its key TTPs include the acquisition of botnet infrastructure (T1583.005), exploitation of remote services (T1210) for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning (T1595.002), and automated exfiltration (T1020) over alternative protocols (T1048). The group is attributed to China and primarily targets critical infrastructure sectors in the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom, with motivations focused on espionage and pre-positioning for potential future disruptive attacks.[/profile]

This artifact is a 64-bit Windows executable file that is packed using UPX. This packed file contains a compiled version of an open-source tool published on GitHub called "FRPC". The "FRPC" is a command-line tool written in Golang that is designed to open a reverse proxy between the compromised system and the TA's C2 server. 

When the "FRPC" is installed and executed on the compromised system, it attempts to establish a connection with the Fast Reverse Proxy Server (FRPS) using the reverse proxy method to allow the TA to control the compromised system. This "FRPC" application supports encryption, compression, and allows easy token authentication. It also supports the protocols below:

--Begin protocols--
Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
User Datagram Protocol (UDP)
An alternative Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
An alternative Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS)
--End protocols--

[common]
	server_addr = 192.168.18.111
	server_port = 8081
	server_addrs = 203.95.9.54,203.95.9.54,203.95.9.54
	server_ports = 8443,8443,8443
	token = 1kyRdFmuk0i25JbCJmtift1c9VA05VBS
	protocol = tcp
	tls_enable = true
	disable_custom_tls_first_byte = true
	log_level = debug
	
	[plugin_socks5]
	type = tcp
	remote_port = 1080

	use_encryption = true
	use_compression = true
